title: Mobile service boundaries, battery and antennas
explanation: Begin with the exact device model and service instructions. Mobile parts may be soldered, adhesively secured, paired to firmware or not intended for field replacement. A laptop RAM socket does not imply that its processor or flash storage is replaceable. Before opening the case, protect data, shut down, disconnect external power and follow the manufacturer’s battery-disconnection and ESD procedure. A swollen or damaged battery is a hazard: stop charging and use the approved handling route rather than squeezing the enclosure shut. Antenna leads are small coaxial connections; route and reconnect them according to their labels and the service guide, because poor placement or a loose connector can degrade radio performance without causing an obvious device-manager error. Cameras, microphones, fingerprint readers and NFC hardware also have privacy or policy controls. Separate physical connection, driver recognition, application permission and organizational policy before deciding a component has failed.
distinctions: Model-specific serviceability
Safe power and ESD handling
Physical connection versus software permission
Post-service verification

example.reasoning: Successful use in another app is evidence that the module and some driver path work. The failing application and its permissions are a narrower boundary.

Assume any radio connection proves the antenna path is correct
Erase all user data to repair radio range
questions.explanation: A damaged, misrouted or disconnected antenna can produce weak range while the radio still associates nearby.

title: Ports, accessories and advertised capabilities
explanation: Identify a connector, then separately establish the supported protocol, data rate, power delivery and alternate modes. USB-C is a reversible connector; a particular port or cable may support only a subset of charging, USB data, DisplayPort alternate mode or Thunderbolt capabilities. A charging-only cable can fit a data port and still fail the desired job. Check the laptop’s supported power input and the charger/cable’s negotiated capability; a high wattage printed on one component does not prove the complete path can supply it. A port replicator typically exposes existing connections; a dock may add hubs, display processing, networking and power features. Display resolution, refresh rate and the number of simultaneous monitors are constrained by the host, dock, cable and protocol. Pairing an accessory also differs from connecting by cable: Bluetooth needs discoverability, the correct device and successful authorization; NFC is short-range interaction rather than a general replacement for Wi-Fi throughput.
distinctions: Connector shape
Data/video protocol
Cable and device capabilities
Power negotiation

reference.meaning: Traditional host/peripheral connector families; shape is not a complete speed specification.
Older small connector families found on legacy peripherals and devices.
Connector that can carry multiple supported modes; verify each device and cable.
A high-speed interface whose generation, certification and host support must be checked.
Apple connector used on supported older devices; verify model and cable support.
Active stylus functions depend on compatible digitizer technology, not merely a touch surface.
Pairing, selected input/output profile, battery and application audio selection all affect operation.
Share a device’s connection by supported USB, Wi-Fi or Bluetooth methods; account for carrier policy and data caps.

example.situation: A dock charges a laptop but its monitors stay blank. What evidence is needed before buying another dock?
example.reasoning: Power and video are separate negotiated capabilities. Every component in the video path must support the requested mode.

options: The host port, cable, dock and display modes support the required video path
A matching USB-C plug proves full video support
More charging wattage always enables video
questions.explanation: Power and video are separate negotiated capabilities. Every component in the video path must support the requested mode.

questions.prompt: A passive stylus moves the pointer, but pressure sensitivity does not work. What should support investigate?
options: Whether the stylus protocol, digitizer and app support active pressure features
Assume all touchscreens support every active stylus
Replace the network card
questions.explanation: Basic capacitive contact does not establish an active stylus protocol or application capability.

title: Cellular, pairing, location and managed synchronization
explanation: Separate the radio connection, internet access, account authentication and application synchronization. A phone can have strong cellular signal yet be unable to use a corporate application because its identity, license or management enrollment is not valid. SIM and eSIM identify a subscriber profile; provisioning, carrier compatibility and plan status still determine usable service. Wi-Fi and cellular are different transports, and hotspot use may have a separate allowance. Bluetooth setup usually requires enabling the radio, discoverability or pairing mode, selecting the intended device, confirming the requested code and testing the required function. Location may use satellite positioning, cellular infrastructure, Wi-Fi-related information and OS services; indoor operation and privacy settings affect results. An MDM policy can control configuration, applications and corporate data differently for BYOD and company-owned devices. Synchronization settings specify what moves, which direction and which account owns it. A sync icon is not proof that every item has reached an independent recoverable copy.
distinctions: Radio and subscriber profile
IP connectivity
Identity and management policy
Application synchronization

reference.meaning: Physical or electronically provisioned subscriber identity profile; not a universal guarantee of carrier access.
Cellular generations with availability and support dependent on carrier, location and device.
Establish and authorize the intended relationship, then test its actual function.
Different sources can contribute to location; privacy controls and environment matter.
Ownership and management policy affect allowed configuration and data separation.
Verify account, scope, timing, capacity and conflicts for each data type.

example.situation: A phone browses normally but work mail stopped after a password change. What is the best next boundary to investigate?
example.reasoning: Working internet narrows the transport question; account and policy evidence can explain application-specific failure.
example.result: The work account’s authentication, enrollment and synchronization error

Assume every internet connection guarantees valid application credentials
questions.explanation: Working internet narrows the transport question; account and policy evidence can explain application-specific failure.

questions.prompt: A user pairs with a nearby device of an unexpected name and is asked for a PIN. What should happen?
options: Verify the intended accessory identity and pairing procedure before authorizing it
Approve every nearby request
Publish the device PIN in a support forum
questions.explanation: Pairing is an authorization action; proximity alone does not identify the correct peripheral.

title: Service ports and what a successful connection proves
explanation: A port number identifies a transport endpoint convention; it does not prove the service is genuine, secure or configured on that default. TCP supplies an ordered byte stream with connection establishment and retransmission. UDP sends datagrams without that same delivery/order guarantee; an application may add its own reliability. DNS commonly uses UDP for ordinary queries and TCP where required, so calling it UDP-only is incorrect. DHCPv4 uses UDP server/client ports 67/68. When diagnosing access, identify client and server, transport, destination port, actual service configuration, route, stateful or stateless filtering and the return path. A firewall change should permit the needed service as narrowly as practicable rather than open every port. An open TCP port is evidence of a listener or intermediary response, not proof of a working login or correct application behavior. Unencrypted legacy protocols should not be confused with encrypted alternatives just because their purpose is similar.
distinctions: Service requirement
Transport and destination port
Forward and return path
Application verification

reference.meaning: 21 is control; traditional active-mode data commonly uses 20, while passive operation uses negotiated data ports.
Remote command-line access; SSH provides encryption, whereas Telnet normally does not.
A common mail-server transport port; submission and protected configurations can use other ports.
Name-service queries and related traffic may use UDP and TCP.

Common web ports; HTTPS uses transport protection when correctly configured.

Legacy NetBIOS services versus direct-hosted SMB, with transport depending on the specific service.
Directory-access and remote-desktop conventions; assess actual security and transport settings.

example.situation: A firewall allows UDP 53 but blocks TCP 53. A DNS problem appears during a response requiring TCP. What is the best conclusion?
example.reasoning: A protocol’s common usage must not be simplified into a false transport restriction.
example.result: The DNS policy may be incomplete; DNS can require TCP as well as UDP

options: The DNS policy may be incomplete; DNS can require TCP as well as UDP
DNS can never use TCP
Opening unrelated RDP traffic fixes DNS by definition
questions.explanation: A protocol’s common usage must not be simplified into a false transport restriction.

questions.prompt: A TCP connection to port 22 succeeds but SSH authentication fails. What does the connection test establish?
options: A transport path responds; the application identity and authentication still need verification
The password is necessarily correct
The target operating system has been fully verified
questions.explanation: Transport reachability and application readiness are different outcomes.

title: Wi-Fi bands, standards, channels and interference
explanation: Radio design trades range, spectrum availability, interference, channel width and client capability. The 2.4 GHz band commonly reaches through obstacles better but is crowded and has limited non-overlapping channel choices. The 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands offer additional spectrum where permitted and supported; higher frequency does not automatically mean greater range. Channel widths increase potential throughput but consume more spectrum and can worsen contention in a dense deployment. Regional rules and device capabilities determine valid channels and power. Wi-Fi 4 corresponds to 802.11n, Wi-Fi 5 to 802.11ac and Wi-Fi 6 to 802.11ax; Wi-Fi 6E extends 802.11ax operation into 6 GHz on compatible equipment. A client and access point must both support the desired band and mode. Bluetooth shares parts of the 2.4 GHz environment. NFC operates at very short range, while RFID describes broader identification systems with technology-dependent range. None of these labels alone proves usable application throughput.
distinctions: Client/AP capability
Permitted band and channel
Interference and signal quality
Measured application performance

reference.meaning: Legacy 5 GHz Wi-Fi.
Legacy 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi families.
Supports 2.4 and/or 5 GHz depending on implementation.
5 GHz Wi-Fi generation.
Wi-Fi 6 uses supported 2.4/5 GHz operation; 6E adds 6 GHz capability.
Spectrum consumed by a channel; a wider channel is not automatically better in a crowded area.
Short-range interaction and radio identification systems respectively; use the specific device standards.

example.reasoning: Radio support is a hardware/driver/regulatory capability, separate from naming and DNS.

questions.explanation: Radio support is a hardware/driver/regulatory capability, separate from naming and DNS.

questions.prompt: A crowded office becomes less stable after every AP is set to the widest channel. What should be reviewed?
options: Channel reuse, interference, width and client density using a survey
Assume more width always improves every client
Disable all authentication to change RF congestion
questions.explanation: Wide channels reduce reuse opportunities and can increase contention; deployment evidence should guide the plan.

title: DNS records, DHCP leases and logical separation
explanation: DNS records have distinct roles: A maps a name to IPv4, AAAA to IPv6, CNAME provides an alias, MX identifies mail exchangers and TXT stores text used by mechanisms such as domain verification and email authentication. SPF describes permitted sending sources, DKIM provides a domain-associated message signature, and DMARC evaluates aligned authentication with policy/reporting; these are complementary rather than interchangeable. DHCP scopes define a pool and options, exclusions prevent allocation from reserved portions, and reservations associate a predictable lease with a client identifier. A lease has a lifecycle; a reservation is not simply any manually configured static address. VLANs divide logical layer-2 broadcast domains, while routing and policy determine permitted inter-VLAN traffic. A VPN protects or establishes a communication path according to its design; it does not automatically grant every application permission. Troubleshooting should separately test link, address, gateway, resolver, destination and application behavior.
distinctions: Client link
Lease and address options
Gateway/routing policy
DNS record and application

Alias to another name; not a separate IP-address field.
Mail exchanger selection, with preference values.
Text data and distinct email authentication/policy functions.
Allocation pool, withheld addresses and client-specific lease assignment.
Logical local-network separation versus a configured virtual communication path.

questions.explanation: Reservations provide predictable DHCP assignment; conflicting static use can create duplicate addresses.

questions.explanation: Email authentication mechanisms address different checks and require correct configuration and interpretation.

title: Appliances, PoE, physical termination and WAN access
explanation: Identify what a device actually does rather than treating every network box as a router. A switch forwards local Ethernet frames; a router forwards packets between IP networks. A wireless access point bridges wireless clients into a network. A firewall permits or denies traffic according to policy, although products often combine several functions. A patch panel is passive cable termination, not a packet-forwarding security device. A modem or access device matches a provider’s physical technology, such as coaxial cable or DSL; fiber services may use an optical network terminal. Power over Ethernet requires a compatible power-sourcing device, powered device, cable plant, per-port capability and total power budget. PoE injectors add power where appropriate switches do not supply it. Managed switches offer configuration and monitoring capabilities that an unmanaged switch typically lacks. WAN choice also involves availability, latency, bandwidth, usage limits and shared failure dependencies, not just the highest advertised download speed.
distinctions: Media termination
Local switching/AP
Routing and security policy
Provider/WAN path

reference.meaning: Inter-network forwarding, local frame forwarding and wireless access have different functions.
Passive termination that supports organized structured cabling.
PoE families with different power capabilities; verify actual device budgets and supported classes.
Access technologies with different physical and operational constraints.
Local, wireless-local, personal, metropolitan, wide-area and storage-area scopes/purposes; SAN is not simply any file-sharing LAN.
Terminate plugs, terminate IDC connections, trace cables, test characteristics and observe traffic using distinct tools.

example.reasoning: Port count and power budget are separate constraints.

title: Display panels, signal paths and image attributes
explanation: A display fault can arise in the panel, backlight, digitizer, signal source, cable, adapter or selected mode. An LCD modulates a backlight; IPS, TN and VA describe panel technologies with different viewing, response and contrast tradeoffs. Mini-LED usually describes a backlight approach for an LCD, whereas OLED uses emissive pixels and does not require the same backlight arrangement. An inverter is associated with certain older fluorescent-backlit designs, not every modern panel. A touch digitizer detects input separately from generating the image, so a clear picture with failed touch is a different boundary from a black display. Resolution describes pixel dimensions; pixel density also depends on physical size. Refresh rate is updates per second, not the same as resolution or achieved game frame rate. Color gamut describes the range of reproducible colors; it does not alone prove calibration accuracy. Verify the entire GPU/port/cable/adapter/display path for the intended resolution, refresh and feature set.
distinctions: Application/GPU output
Port and supported signal mode
Cable/adapter path
Panel, light and touch components

reference.meaning: Different liquid-crystal panel approaches; compare use-case tradeoffs rather than assigning one universal winner.
Emissive pixels; image-retention/burn-in concerns differ from LCD backlight faults.
A fine-grained backlight approach, commonly paired with LCD technology.
Touch/input sensing component; can fail separately from the visible image.
Pixel dimensions, pixels per physical unit, refresh frequency and color range measure different attributes.

example.reasoning: Image production and touch sensing are separate functions that can fail independently.

The monitor label overrides every cable and adapter limit

questions.explanation: Every relevant component in the path must support the requested signal configuration.

title: Cable media, connector identification and installation constraints
explanation: Connector recognition is only the first step in selecting a cable. Verify the electrical or optical interface, bandwidth, distance, environmental rating and device requirements. Twisted-pair category ratings describe supported performance under specified installation conditions; poor termination or excessive length can invalidate the intended link. T568A and T568B are pair-to-pin schemes: a consistently terminated straight-through run uses the same scheme at both ends. A plenum rating concerns fire/smoke suitability for specified air-handling spaces, not higher network speed. Shielding and direct-burial ratings solve different environmental requirements. Fiber selection includes single-mode or multimode media, optic wavelength, reach and connector/polish compatibility; a fitting connector alone is insufficient. Video adapters may be active or passive and directional. Legacy connectors remain relevant when supporting installed equipment, but should not be mistaken for evidence of current performance or security features.
distinctions: Physical connector
Protocol and media type
Distance/performance specification
Environmental and installation rating

reference.meaning: Common telephone-style versus Ethernet twisted-pair connector families; identify the actual pinout and use.
Threaded coaxial connector commonly associated with cable/RF systems.
Fiber connector families with different mechanical forms; media and optics still must match.
Legacy serial-style connector family; the physical shell alone does not specify every signal pinout.
Distinct power connection families; do not force a connector or assume adapter quality.
Digital audio/video, display-interface, legacy digital/mixed variants and analog video families respectively.
Internal and external serial storage interfaces; data signaling and power delivery must be considered separately.
Protocol families with different throughput capabilities; versions and lanes matter independently of connector shape.
Different fiber propagation designs paired with suitable optics.
Fire/smoke, interference and outdoor-environment constraints are separate ratings.

example.reasoning: Environmental rating and signal-performance rating answer different selection questions.

title: DDR generations, form factors, ECC and channels
explanation: A memory purchase must match the processor, board, firmware and physical form factor. DDR generations use different electrical and mechanical standards and are not freely interchangeable. DIMM commonly refers to desktop/server modules; SO-DIMM is a smaller form used by many portable systems, while some devices have soldered memory instead. ECC capability requires a compatible platform and supported module type; ECC, registered/buffered design and capacity are related selection dimensions, not synonyms. Multiple memory channels can improve bandwidth when supported modules are populated according to the vendor’s rules. Two modules installed in adjacent slots do not necessarily mean the desired channel configuration is active. Capacity, supported speeds, timings, rank/population constraints and firmware support can affect stability. A module’s advertised speed is not proof the whole platform will run it at that setting. Diagnose failures with power isolated, seating and compatibility checks, vendor POST indicators and appropriate memory tests; do not assume every crash is caused by RAM.
distinctions: CPU memory controller
Board/firmware support
Compatible modules and population
Tested operating configuration

reference.meaning: Match the supported generation; physical notches and electrical requirements differ.
Physical form factors; device serviceability and exact platform support still matter.
Error-correction capability versus its absence; platform support is required.
Independent data path from controller to memory; population rules determine usable arrangements.
The negotiated stable configuration can differ from a module’s marketing specification.

title: Storage interfaces, RAID calculations and recovery boundaries
explanation: Separate storage media, form factor and interface. A rotating HDD has mechanical latency and may be described by spindle speed and a 2.5-inch or 3.5-inch form factor. SSDs remove rotating media but still differ in controller, interface, workload suitability and endurance. NVMe commonly uses PCIe; SATA uses a different protocol path. M.2 and mSATA are form factors/interfaces that require exact platform support, and a physically fitting module is not proof of protocol compatibility. SAS is a storage interface used in compatible systems. RAID changes performance and fault-tolerance properties across disks, but does not protect against every controller failure, deletion, malware event or site loss. Calculate usable capacity from the level and smallest member size, then separately consider rebuild exposure and performance. Always verify the actual implementation’s supported failure combinations and procedures rather than assuming a simple drive-count rule covers every array state.
distinctions: Media/form factor
Protocol/controller path
Array layout and fault tolerance
Independent recovery copy

reference.meaning: Striping; usable capacity is normally the sum of equal-sized members, with no redundancy.
Mirroring; a basic two-disk mirror normally provides one member’s usable capacity and tolerates one member failure.
Distributed single parity; normally (N−1) × smallest member size, with at least three disks and one-disk failure tolerance.
Dual parity; normally (N−2) × smallest member size, with at least four disks and two-disk failure tolerance.
Stripe of mirrored pairs; normally half of equal-sized raw capacity, requiring at least four disks. Surviving multiple failures depends on which mirrors lose members.
Different interface/protocol families; check the full controller and device path.
Removable media differ in endurance, interface and supported use; no medium is automatically a verified backup.

example.reasoning: Single parity consumes the equivalent of one member: (4−1) × 2 TB = 6 TB.

title: Motherboards, firmware, CPU architecture and trusted boot
explanation: Platform compatibility is a chain: chassis and board form factor, power connections, CPU socket and supported processor list, firmware revision, memory and expansion capabilities, and thermal design all matter. ATX, microATX and ITX describe board-format families, not universal feature guarantees. PCIe links have lane and generation constraints; a connector’s physical length does not guarantee that every lane is electrically available. Firmware boot order and the chosen boot mode must match the installed system. UEFI is a modern firmware interface; Secure Boot checks authorized boot components under its trust configuration, while a TPM can protect keys and record measurements. Neither feature is a replacement for updates or backups. A firmware setup password and an OS account password protect different boundaries. x86/x64 and ARM are architecture families with software compatibility implications; more cores do not automatically accelerate a single-threaded workload. Virtualization support must be present, enabled where required and compatible with the selected hypervisor.
distinctions: Chassis/board/power fit
CPU/firmware/memory compatibility
Boot trust and key protection
OS and workload compatibility

reference.meaning: Board form-factor families affecting fit and expansion; consult the exact model.
Distinct expansion and connection mechanisms with model-specific lane and protocol limits.
Firmware selection of supported boot paths; wrong order can resemble a missing OS.
Authorized boot-component verification under a configured trust policy.
Hardware-backed cryptographic capabilities with different form factors and deployment purposes.
Architecture families; application, driver and OS compatibility must be verified.
Different heat-transfer and removal elements; assembly and maintenance are model-specific.

Virtual machines provide virtual hardware and run guest operating systems; containers commonly share a host kernel and isolate processes through OS mechanisms. Legacy or cross-platform workloads still require architecture, driver and application compatibility checks; virtualization is not universal instruction-set translation. A VM snapshot captures a point-in-time state but may depend on the original storage and does not replace an independent tested backup. A sandbox’s usefulness depends on its actual isolation, shared folders, clipboard, network mode and host protections. title: Malware behaviors, detection and controlled recovery
explanation: Classify observable behavior without treating a label as complete attribution. A virus attaches to suitable host content, a worm can propagate, a Trojan misrepresents its purpose, spyware and stalkerware monitor activity, and a keylogger records input. Rootkits can conceal or alter system visibility; boot-sector and fileless techniques target different execution/persistence paths. Ransomware can both disrupt access and steal data, while a cryptominer consumes resources for mining. Adware and potentially unwanted programs may be intrusive without every instance meeting the same malware definition. Antivirus, anti-malware, EDR, MDR and XDR describe different detection, telemetry and managed-response capabilities rather than interchangeable product guarantees. Follow the organization’s incident process: verify symptoms, contain as appropriate, preserve evidence, eradicate or rebuild, restore safely, update controls and verify behavior afterward. Physical destruction must meet the approved standard and must not create unsafe handling or environmental harm. Outsourcing does not remove accountability: identify media, maintain custody records, define the required outcome, obtain appropriate evidence and verify the vendor process. A certificate by itself should be checked against the actual assets and scope. Real sanitization is destructive and requires explicit authorization and verified targets.

title: Backup chains, RPO/RTO and proving restoration
explanation: A backup strategy begins with what must be recovered, how much data loss is acceptable, how quickly service must return and which dependencies restoration requires. A differential normally captures changes since the last full, so a conventional restore uses that full plus the selected differential. Product terminology and application consistency must be checked in the actual system. A scheduled job reporting success proves less than a restoration test that checks the required files, application state, permissions and usable result. RPO concerns tolerated data loss measured in time, while RTO concerns the target duration to restore service. Copies on the same failed storage or accessible to the same destructive identity may share a failure mode. Encryption keys, catalogs, credentials, network access and recovery media are dependencies that can be forgotten until an outage. A service restart may interrupt users; a reimaging or deletion loop can destroy data at scale. Test with nonproduction inputs and the least required permissions. AI assistance can suggest commands and explain errors, but it can hallucinate syntax, infer the wrong environment or expose sensitive input to an external service. Public and private deployments have different data-handling arrangements that must be verified, not assumed from a product label. Review output against trusted documentation and observed state. Automation does not turn an unsupported guess into evidence, and an AI-generated plan still requires authorization for real side effects.

explanation: A server role describes a service, not necessarily a dedicated physical computer. One host can run several services, and one service can span many hosts. DNS answers name queries, DHCP leases configuration, a file server shares stored resources, a print server queues jobs, and a mail server handles defined mail functions. A database service stores and retrieves structured application data under its own access model. Syslog transports event messages; NTP supports time synchronization. AAA separates authentication, authorization and accounting, which can be provided through coordinated services. A proxy mediates selected requests, a load balancer distributes traffic, and a spam gateway evaluates mail. UTM products combine functions but still need correct policy. Legacy and embedded devices, including SCADA and IoT systems, may have unusual uptime, safety, patching and vendor-support constraints. Do not apply a disruptive desktop repair to an industrial device without understanding its process role and authorized maintenance procedure.

title: Application architecture, dependencies, deployment and business impact
explanation: Installation success depends on architecture, OS version, supported dependencies, licensing, privileges and resources. A 32-bit versus 64-bit requirement is not interchangeable with the storage size of an installer. Graphics-intensive work can require supported GPU capabilities and video memory as well as system RAM and CPU capacity. Hardware tokens, driver support and external devices can be application dependencies. A downloadable package, mounted ISO, physical medium and managed image are distribution methods rather than automatic trust guarantees. Obtain software through approved sources and verify applicable signatures or hashes against trusted references. Installation can modify services, drivers, file associations, network traffic and shared runtimes, affecting other users or applications. Plan testing, communication, authorization and recovery appropriate to the business impact. Do not turn off security controls merely because an installer asks; establish the actual compatibility or policy issue first.

explanation: Cloud productivity combines application, account, licensing, storage, sharing and network dependencies. Identity synchronization coordinates supported account information between systems; it is not the same operation as synchronizing files. Folder sync can be selective, delayed, conflicted or restricted by capacity and policy. A local cached file may remain available offline while a newer cloud version has not arrived. Calendar, mail, instant messaging, meetings and shared documents each have their own settings and user expectations. Version history can help recover changes but must be distinguished from an independent backup and applicable retention guarantees. Before broadening sharing to solve access denied, identify the intended recipient and minimum permission. Verify both directions of a sync workflow with harmless test content rather than assuming an icon means everything is complete.

title: Physical barriers, identity factors and access mechanisms
explanation: Physical security addresses entry, movement, equipment access and evidence. Bollards restrict vehicle paths, fences and locks define barriers, vestibules can control sequential entry, and guards provide human observation and response. Cameras, alarms and motion sensors detect or deter under a configured process but do not all physically block an intrusion. Badge readers, keys, smart cards, mobile credentials and biometrics use different identity and possession characteristics. Biometric use also raises enrollment, matching-error, privacy and fallback questions. Logical access uses subjects, resources and rules: least privilege limits permissions, ACLs specify applicable access, and zero trust rejects unconditional trust based only on location. MFA combines different factor categories; two passwords or password plus PIN normally remain knowledge factors. SSO reduces repeated sign-ins through an identity arrangement but does not eliminate authorization. SAML is one federation-related assertion mechanism; just-in-time privileged access limits standing authority under a controlled workflow.

title: Wireless protection, RADIUS, TACACS+ and Kerberos distinctions
explanation: Wireless security mode, encryption and identity backend are related but separate choices. WPA2 and WPA3 describe security generations with personal and enterprise arrangements; support depends on clients, infrastructure and configuration. AES-based modern protection should not be confused with older TKIP, and a hidden SSID is not a cryptographic control. In enterprise access, 802.1X coordinates port-based authentication using an authenticator and an authentication service with a suitable EAP method. RADIUS is commonly used as an AAA protocol in network access. TACACS+ is often associated with device-administration AAA and separates functions differently from RADIUS; use the platform’s documented support. Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication system with dependencies such as trusted identities, service naming and time. It is not simply a wireless cipher. Verify certificates and the expected authentication server where the design requires them; otherwise an apparently familiar network name can mislead users into trusting an unintended endpoint.

title: Social engineering and application/network threat boundaries
explanation: Identify the mechanism and evidence before assigning a confident attack label. Phishing can arrive through email, text, voice or QR codes; spear phishing narrows targeting and whaling focuses on high-value roles. Impersonation, pretexting, shoulder surfing, tailgating and discarded-material collection exploit different human or physical boundaries. BEC can use a compromised account or convincing impersonation without an obvious malicious attachment. A rogue wireless lookalike is a different path from an application injection flaw. SQL injection changes a database-command context, while XSS introduces script into a browser execution context; both require context-appropriate preventive controls. Denial of service targets availability, and distributed sources do not make every outage a DDoS event. Credential guessing, replay, spoofing and on-path observation/alteration have different preconditions. An unpatched or end-of-life system is a weakness or risk condition, not proof that a specific exploit succeeded. Preserve evidence and follow authorized reporting rather than testing against unrelated systems.

title: Exam cleanup sequence versus real incident authority
explanation: Know the sequence and the reason behind a controlled malware response without applying it blindly. The A+ objective presents a simplified small-office cleanup flow: investigate symptoms, quarantine, manage the relevant Windows Home restore state, remediate, update anti-malware, use appropriate scan environments, reimage/reinstall where required, schedule ongoing protection, restore the relevant recovery configuration and educate the user. In an actual organization, the authorized incident plan, evidence preservation, legal requirements and recovery policy determine what a technician may change. Disabling recovery or deleting infected files can destroy evidence or remove a needed restore option, so it is not an automatic first step in every incident. Isolation must be scoped and coordinated to limit spread while preserving required access for responders. A trusted rebuild can be preferable when confidence in cleanup is inadequate. Recovery is not complete until the original entry point, persistence, affected identities and post-restoration operation have been addressed.

Use supported updates, appropriate endpoint protection, an intentional service set and restricted administrative authority. Screen-lock timeouts, account expiration, failed-attempt handling and permitted sign-in times address different risks and must follow policy. Long, unique credentials and protected password-manager use are more important than reusing a predictable pattern across accounts; do not treat routine forced password changes as a universal substitute for compromise detection. Data-at-rest encryption needs an approved recovery-key process; otherwise a hardware or firmware change can become a data-loss event. AutoRun and removable-media behavior should match policy. Preserve user data and required business services while testing the baseline, and verify effective settings rather than only the intended template.

Rooting or jailbreaking can change the platform’s trust and support assumptions; developer mode is not identical to a confirmed compromise. Application and OS updates have separate channels and eligibility. Lost-device actions such as location, remote lock or wipe require authorized scope and an understanding of connectivity, data consequences and platform behavior. A wipe command being issued is not proof it executed. Backups, account-session control, token revocation and documented follow-up can remain necessary even when device recovery is unlikely.

UPnP or other automatic mapping features can change exposure depending on implementation and policy; review the actual behavior rather than assuming convenience equals authorization. Wireless settings include supported encryption, guest policy and placement. Hiding an SSID does not establish secrecy or access control. A valid HTTPS connection protects a transport relationship with the named site under its trust model; it does not prove the site is honest or the content is harmless. Certificate warnings need investigation of name, trust, date and possible interception rather than routine bypass. Private browsing limits selected local persistence but does not make activity invisible to sites, employers or network operators. Clearing cache, cookies, history and synchronized account data affects different things. Secure DNS, proxy settings, pop-up controls and content blocking also have distinct scopes and policy implications.

A no-OS message can reflect boot selection or storage visibility, not necessarily erased files. Stop errors can involve drivers, hardware or kernel-level components; collect the code, timing, recent changes and available diagnostic evidence before choosing a fix. A service that fails to start may have dependency, identity, configuration or resource problems. Slow profile load can involve local profile state, network resources and policy processing. Time drift can affect logs and authentication, so do not treat a corrected clock display as the entire root-cause analysis. Memory pressure and USB-controller resource warnings are different from disk capacity exhaustion. Startup repair, restore points, driver rollback and a clean rebuild have different purposes and data/availability impacts. Choose the least speculative supported recovery that fits the observed boundary, with backups and recovery material ready.

title: Expansion cards, CPU execution and cooling components
explanation: Match expansion hardware to both the physical platform and the workload. A network interface card adds supported network connectivity; a sound card handles audio functions; a graphics card supplies display/rendering capabilities; a capture card ingests supported external media signals. One device can combine roles, but a similar port does not guarantee the same function or direction. Integrated graphics can share system resources, whereas a dedicated GPU has its own design and may include dedicated VRAM. CPU architecture affects OS, application and driver compatibility; x86, x64 and ARM labels are not just relative performance rankings. Core count, clock behavior, thermal/power limits and application parallelism affect performance together. Multisocket systems introduce additional platform and software constraints. Cooling uses heat-transfer interfaces and heat-removal components: a heat sink and fan, thermal paste or a specified pad, and potentially liquid-loop parts. Incorrect assembly, blocked airflow or failed fans can cause throttling or shutdown even when the processor itself is not defective.

Integrated/dedicated graphics: Resource and feature requirements differ.
Architecture/cores/workload: Compatibility and parallelism are separate from marketing speed.
Paste/pad/heat sink/fan/liquid: Different elements of a thermal path.

title: Display symptom matrix and meaningful next observations
explanation: A symptom matrix should generate a testable hypothesis, not declare a cause from one appearance. A blank screen can reflect power, input, cable, mode, GPU or panel problems. A faint but present image suggests a different path from no image at all. A dead pixel, burn-in or image retention is not the same as a software window being stuck. Flicker can involve refresh settings, a signal path, power or a component fault; reproduce it and change one controlled variable. Incorrect color can result from a cable/channel problem, settings or the display. A fuzzy image may involve scaling, focus, resolution or optics rather than a universally failed panel. Projector shutdown has thermal and light-source considerations, while sizing and keystone concerns relate to placement and supported geometry. Audio over a display path additionally depends on the selected output device, cable/adapter and supported signal mode. Model-specific tests and a known-good path provide stronger evidence than replacing parts based on an isolated adjective.

title: Printer image, feed, queue and finishing symptoms
explanation: Printer symptoms span independent subsystems. Lines, speckling, repeated/echo images, faded output and unfused toner call for technology-specific image-path evidence. Paper jams, skew, no feed and multipage feeding concern media type, guides, rollers, separation or obstructions. A grinding noise or repeated alarm is a reason to stop and use the service procedure, not force movement. Stapling and hole-punch finishing add their own paper-path and accessory-state dependencies. An unrecognized tray can involve installation, configuration, driver capabilities or sensing, while incorrect orientation can be a job-setting mismatch. Multiple pending jobs or a frozen queue can arise in a client/server spooler or at the device; determine where the state exists before clearing every job. Connectivity and secure-release policy can also delay output without an image-engine fault. Compare a local device test, different clients and representative jobs, then verify image, feed and finishing functions that the user actually needs.

title: Desktop and mobile OS families, application models and lifecycle
explanation: OS families have different application formats, drivers, management tools, security models and supported hardware. Windows, macOS, Linux and Chrome OS are not interchangeable solely because each presents a browser and files. Chrome OS devices may support additional application environments depending on model, version and policy; do not assume every device supports every Android or Linux workload. iOS, iPadOS and Android have mobile application and management arrangements that differ from a traditional desktop administrator model. Apple desktop software must match supported hardware and architecture, while Linux distributions differ in packaging, services and support policies. Compatibility includes application dependencies, file formats, peripherals, required identity services and management controls. Vendor end-of-life and update limitations affect whether a configuration remains supported; successful boot is not evidence of ongoing servicing eligibility. A support plan should distinguish keeping a legacy workload functional from approving a new unsupported deployment, with migration or isolation decisions made through the organization’s process.

title: Synthetic fulls, rotation, copy placement and restoration targets
explanation: A synthetic full is assembled by a backup system from existing backup data and subsequent changes according to the product’s design, rather than necessarily rereading the entire source dataset as a traditional new full would. Its usability still depends on the integrity and availability of the required backup information and metadata. Rotation schemes such as grandfather-father-son organize retention across generations; they do not by themselves establish an adequate number of independent copies or meet every recovery objective. The common 3-2-1 principle describes maintaining multiple copies, different media or storage failure boundaries and an offsite copy, but actual resilience depends on access control, isolation, immutability where appropriate and tested restoration. Onsite copies can support speed while offsite copies address some location-specific risks. In-place recovery can overwrite current data; an alternate-location restore can support inspection and comparison before replacement. Select and verify the target deliberately, including permissions, application consistency and the possibility of restoring unwanted or compromised content.

GFS/retention: A rotation policy, not proof of independent failure domains.
Onsite/offsite/3-2-1: Placement and copy-diversity principles need real control verification.
In-place/alternate location: Different overwrite and comparison implications.
